evidenceAudit.scope: Adults who may be in the last days of life in hospital, hospice or home: recognising dying, communication and shared decisions, hydration, stopping non-beneficial treatment, and anticipatory symptom control. Verified against NICE NG31 and Saudi MOH Protocol-010 (Palliative Care — End of Life Care).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Midazolam, glycopyrronium, hyoscine and SC haloperidol doses — local formulary
SFDA registration not checked per drug

pathophysiology.summary: In the last days of life progressive organ failure reduces consciousness, oral intake and circulation. Care shifts to comfort, dignity and support for the person and family, while staying alert to reversible changes or temporary recovery.
keyMechanisms: Falling cerebral perfusion and metabolic failure reduce consciousness and can cause agitation or delirium.
Reduced swallowing and cough allow pharyngeal secretions to pool — noisy breathing, which is usually not distressing to the person (NICE NG31).
Circulatory failure produces mottled skin and Cheyne–Stokes breathing.
Drug handling changes with renal and hepatic failure — start low, titrate, and prefer SC or IV routes over IM (NICE NG31).

symptoms: Increasing fatigue, loss of appetite, reduced communication and mobility, social withdrawal (NICE NG31 1.1.2).
Pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety, agitation, noisy secretions.
physicalSigns: Deteriorating consciousness, Cheyne–Stokes breathing, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions, progressive weight loss (NICE NG31 1.1.2).
Signs of reversible problems: urinary retention, full rectum, dehydration.
redFlags: Improvement in signs or function — may be stabilising or recovering; reassess (NICE NG31 1.1.3)
Uncontrolled symptoms or unwanted sedation — specialist palliative care
Catastrophic bleeding risk where a blood count would change care
Family distress or disagreement about goals
precipitants: Progressive advanced illness (cancer, organ failure, frailty, dementia)

differentials.condition: Reversible deterioration (sepsis, hypercalcaemia, opioid toxicity, dehydration)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Recent change with a treatable cause consistent with goals.

differentials.condition: Delirium from urinary retention or constipation
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Agitation that settles once the bladder or rectum is relieved (NICE NG31 1.5.23).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and communicate
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as dying is suspected
actions: Gather physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs, goals and wishes, and the views of those important to the person (NICE NG31 1.1.1).
Explain uncertainty honestly; identify the person's preferences, advance statements and anticipatory prescribing decisions.
Seek more experienced advice if signs are ambiguous or conflicting.

clinicalManagement.title: Review medicines
actions: Stop medicines that give no symptom benefit or may harm, after discussion (NICE NG31 1.5.1).

Steroids: continue at a convenient SC dose for serious symptom control; stop if given recently/low dose for appetite; if long term continue a physiological dose of dexamethasone 1 mg (MOH Protocol-010 p. 4).
Fentanyl patch: leave in place and change on schedule; add a syringe driver for extra opioid needs (MOH Protocol-010 p. 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Anticipatory symptom control
actions: Use SC or IV routes — avoid IM (NICE NG31 1.5.5). Start low in opioid-naïve people and titrate (1.5.7).
Pain: opioid matched to severity; IV morphine 2.5–5 mg every 3–4 h as a starting dose (MOH Protocol-010 p. 9).
Breathlessness: opioid and/or benzodiazepine; oxygen only for symptomatic hypoxaemia (NICE NG31 1.5.16–1.5.17).
Nausea: antiemetic by cause (see Nausea topic); obstructive bowel: hyoscine butylbromide, then octreotide if no response in 24 h (NICE NG31 1.5.22).
Agitation/anxiety: benzodiazepine trial; delirium: antipsychotic trial (NICE NG31 1.5.26–1.5.27).

Noisy secretions: reassure; if distressing use atropine, glycopyrronium, hyoscine butylbromide or hyoscine hydrobromide; review every 4–12 h and change or stop after 12 h if no effect (NICE NG31 1.5.31–1.5.33).
More than 2–3 PRN doses in 24 h: syringe pump (NICE NG31 1.5.6).

clinicalManagement.title: Hydration and mouth care
actions: Support drinking if wished and able; mouth care for dry mouth.
Discuss benefits and harms of clinically assisted hydration; trial if thirst or delirium may be due to dehydration; stop if fluid overload (NICE NG31 1.4).

learningObjectives: Recognise the last days of life and provide anticipatory, comfort-focused care with the person and family.

keyPoints: Recognise dying, but watch for improvement.
SC or IV, never IM; start low.
Syringe pump if more than 2–3 PRN doses/day.
pitfalls: Routine bloods and observations that do not change care.
Missing urinary retention as a cause of agitation.
Removing a fentanyl patch in the last days.

patientEducation: Explain expected changes such as noisy breathing and reduced intake.
Invite family involvement in mouth care and comfort.
lifestyleAndDiet: Comfort-focused: positioning, mouth care, quiet environment.
dischargeCriteria: Not applicable — care continues in the preferred place; rapid transfer home if wished and feasible.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Reassess at least every 24 h and after each new medicine; specialist palliative care if symptoms do not improve promptly or sedation is unwanted (NICE NG31 1.5.9).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Agitation, Cheyne–Stokes breathing, falling consciousness, mottled skin, noisy secretions, weight loss
More than 2–3 PRN doses in 24 h

regimens.indication: Pain or breathlessness in the last days (opioid-naïve)
regimens.duration: Titrate; consider syringe pump if more than 2–3 doses/24 h
regimens.sourceTitle: Protocols for Palliative Care Patients — End of Life Care (MOH Protocol-010)

contraindications: Acute or severe asthma without monitoring/resuscitation
Known or suspected GI obstruction including paralytic ileus

regimens.dose: 0.5–2 mg (FDA label initial range for moderate symptoms; geriatric/debilitated same range)
adjustments: NICE NG31 recommends an antipsychotic trial but gives no dose; label dose is for psychosis — off-label in delirium

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG31 names drug classes for each symptom but gives no doses; MOH Protocol-010 gives morphine and steroid end-of-life doses. Midazolam, antisecretory and SC antipsychotic doses must come from the local palliative formulary. Check SFDA registration and controlled-drug rules.
